title: Zechariah
summary: Zechariah is a biblical book focused on visions, temple restoration, priestly and royal hope, and future renewal.
historical_context: Zechariah encourages the restored community with visions of temple rebuilding, cleansing, and royal hope.
ancient_near_east_context: Zechariah belongs to the ancient Mediterranean and Near Eastern world reflected in its setting, institutions, and canonical placement.
hebraic_worldview: Zechariah should be read with attention to covenant memory, communal identity, worship, wisdom, and accountability before the Lord.
second_temple_context: Second Temple readers received Zechariah as part of Israel's Scriptures and read it within questions of identity, worship, exile, and hope.
canonical_context: Within Minor Prophets, book 11 of 12, Zechariah contributes to the Bible's unfolding witness by connecting visions, temple restoration, priestly and royal hope, and future renewal to the larger storyline.
later_christian_reception: Christian interpretation has read Zechariah as part of the canonical witness to faithfulness, judgment, mercy, and hope in Christ-centered Scripture reading.
literary_context: Zechariah uses prophecy, apocalyptic within Minor Prophets, book 11 of 12 to develop its themes through the book's structure and key passages.
covenantal_significance: Zechariah helps readers trace covenant faithfulness, failure, mercy, and hope within its canonical setting.
authorship_positions: Traditional prophetic attribution to the named prophet
Many scholars recognize collection and editorial shaping
date_ranges: 8th-5th centuries BCE, depending on the prophet
Final forms often reflect later collection and editing
original_audience: Israel and Judah under covenant accountability before and after exile
historical_setting: Assyrian, Babylonian, and post-exilic settings across the prophetic corpus
canonical_role: Zechariah anchors visions, temple restoration, priestly and royal hope, and future renewal within Minor Prophets, book 11 of 12 and connects the book to related people, places, events, and themes.
interpretive_disputes: How to read prophetic poetry, irony, and symbolic action

Temple rebuilding frames the early prophetic messages.
The book belongs to the post-exilic return setting.
Royal and priestly hope contribute to messianic readings.
Restoration hope runs through the visions and promises.
